newsitem.title: USA: Brokerages downgrade AT&T, stock falls.
newsitem.headline: Brokerages downgrade AT&T, stock falls.

text.p: Two major Wall Street brokerages lowered their earnings estimates for AT&T Corp. Monday amid intensifying competition in the industry, sparking a heavy sell-off of the stock.
The stock fell $2.25 to $39.25 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the second most-active issue at mid-afternoon.

Salomon Brothers anaylst Jack Grubman, citing higher spending and greater competition in the telecommunications market, cut AT&T's 1997 earnings estimate to $3.00 per share from $3.60 and 1998 estimate to $3.25 per share from $3.80.
Fourth-quarter 1996 earnings per share will be closer to 70 cents than the previously forecast of 78 cents, he added.
Grubman said his new estimates may "still be too high," but continued to recommend holding AT&T stock.
AT&T reported third-quarter profits of $1.4 billion, or 89 cents a share, on revenues of $13.2 billion.
First Boston Corp. also lowered its AT&T earnings estimates, but no details were immediately available.
AT&T said it does not comment on stock activity or analysts' reports.
"We have not yet determined what 1997 will bring, but it is safe to say we do not agree with the more pessimistic comments," said a source at AT&T who declined to be identified.
The source acknowledged the company was facing stiff competition from traditional rivals like MCI Communications Corp. as well as small aggressive competitors and soon, the regional Bells.
Separately, AT&T said it won a $341 million contract from Delta Air Lines Inc. for worldwide voice and data services.

The seven-year contract extends an existing agreement between the two under which AT&T provides a virtual network for the airline. The new contract will provide Delta with intelligent call-processing to reduce reservation backlogs.

In another announcement, a partner in an African consortium that is bidding to take over Ivory Coast's telephone company Ci-Telcom said AT&T has agreed to buy a 35 percent stake in the consortium, Africa Bell.
Ci-Telcom, with an estimated value of between $200 million to $350 million, is the most important company on Ivory Coast's privatisation programme.

AT&T's involvement, if the Africa Bell bid succeeds, would represent a major breakthrough for an American company in a traditionally French domain. Ivory Coast is the most important economy in France's former colonies in West and Central Africa.
